answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1729–1797 · Whig MP, orator and political philosopher
answer.sourceLine: Burke said it in the House of Commons on 7 February 1771, backing a motion for leave to bring in a bill to fix the rights of electors after the Commons had thrown out John Wilkes. His own sentence is longer than the poster version: “First, because the greater the power, the more dangerous the abuse.” The text survives among Burke’s manuscript papers and is printed in his collected Works ↗.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Speech Relative to the Middlesex Election
The Works of the Right Honorable Edmund Burke, vol. VII (Boston: Little, Brown, 1877), p. 62
From Burke’s own preserved manuscript papers, published after his death

source.excerpt: The substance of the question is, to put bounds to your own power by the rules and principles of law. This is, I am sensible, a difficult thing to the corrupt, grasping, and ambitious part of human nature. But the very difficulty argues and enforces the necessity of it. First, because the greater the power, the more dangerous the abuse. Since the Revolution, at least, the power of the nation has all flowed with a full tide into the House of Commons. Secondly, because the House of Commons, as it is the most powerful, is the most corruptible part of the whole Constitution.
trail: 1769 — The quarrel behind the speech. The Commons expelled the radical John Wilkes, voided his re-election three times, and seated his beaten rival Henry Luttrell, who had polled 296 votes to Wilkes’s 1,143. Middlesex election affair ↗

7 February 1771 — Burke speaks for a motion for leave to bring in a bill to ascertain the rights of the electors. The motion is rejected, 167 to 103. His text runs: “First, because the greater the power, the more dangerous the abuse.” Works, vol. VII ↗

Posthumous printing — Burke’s editors record that he had meant to publish some of his Parliamentary speeches and kept fragments and detached notes toward it; the Middlesex Election speech was among those “found in the same imperfect state.” What we read is his own preserved text, not a reporter’s transcript. editors’ note ↗
Television — the shortened line reached a new audience through Criminal Minds, where Jennifer Jareau recites it, credited to Burke, in the season-nine episode “The Return.” Wikiquote ↗
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the 1886 Cassell edition of Thoughts on the Present Discontents, and Speeches; the same sentences read identically in the 1877 Little, Brown Works, vol. VII, p. 62.

author.name: Edmund Burke
author.heading: Edmund Burke
author.metaLine: 1729–1797 · Anglo-Irish MP, orator and founder of modern conservatism
author.bio: Edmund Burke was an Anglo-Irish writer, philosopher and politician, widely credited as the founder of the cultural and political philosophy of conservatism. He sat in the House of Commons as a Rockingham Whig for Wendover, then Bristol, then Malton, and made his name as an orator on the American colonies, the government of India, and the limits of Parliament’s own power. Much of what we quote from him survives not as reported speech but as manuscript he kept himself — including this line.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The name is right — this really is Burke. What travels badly is everything around it: the line is quoted almost everywhere with no work, no date and no context, and in a form Burke did not quite write.

items.why: Burke’s sentence begins “First, because…” It is the first of two numbered reasons for binding the Commons by law — the second being that the Commons “as it is the most powerful, is the most corruptible part of the whole Constitution” — not a free-standing epigram. 1886 Cassell text ↗
BrainyQuote’s page for the line gives Burke’s birth and death dates and his nationality — and no speech, no work, no year at all. see the page ↗

The Burke line is often shelved beside “power tends to corrupt and absolute power corrupts absolutely” — but that is Lord Acton, writing to Bishop Mandell Creighton in 1887. Different man, different sentence. Liberty Fund ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Burke did say it — in the House of Commons on 7 February 1771 — and his own sentence opens “First, because…” The Works of Edmund Burke, vol. VII ↗

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: In 1769 the House of Commons expelled the radical John Wilkes, voided his re-election three times running, and finally handed the Middlesex seat to Henry Luttrell — a man the county had beaten by 1,143 votes to 296. The affair ↗ amounted to the Commons claiming a power to decide who was allowed to sit in it, with no law saying so.

On 7 February 1771 Burke rose to support a motion for leave to bring in a bill that would write the electors’ rights into law. He was not arguing that the Commons was uniquely wicked; he was arguing the opposite — that because so much of the nation’s power had drained into that one chamber, that chamber above all needed a line drawn round it. The famous sentence is the load-bearing beam of that argument.
context.detailsSummary: How this speech survived at all
detailsBody: The text reaches us in an unusual way. Burke’s editors explain that he had intended to publish several of his Parliamentary speeches and had kept fragments and detached notes toward that end; the Middlesex Election speech was among those “found in the same imperfect state” in his manuscript papers. What is printed is therefore Burke’s own preserved wording rather than a shorthand writer’s record of the chamber. the editors’ note ↗

He lost. The editors’ headnote to the speech records that the motion — for leave to bring in a bill to ascertain the rights of the electors in respect to the eligibility of persons to serve in Parliament — was rejected by 167 votes to 103.
context.pull: Our judgments stink in the nostrils of the people.
